speechtext:
Let us suppose that I have a flock of sheep. All hon. members know that some sheep are very prolific while others are not. One ewe may produce one lamb, others may produce two, and others may have triplets. That is a matter beyond the regulation of mankind. What are we to do with the excess numbers? Are we to kill them? Then, the Minister of Agriculture knows perfectly well the uncertainties in connection with the rearing of little pigs. These are some matters beyond our control.
I do not wish to trespass unduly, but I should like to conclude with only one remark. Perhaps the most obnoxious part of the bill appears at page 3. It is as follows:
The board shall, subject to the provisions of this act, have power-
(g) to require full information relating to the production and marketing of the natural product from all persons engaged therein and to require periodic returns to be made by such persons, and inspect the books and premises of such persons.
Marketing Act-Mr. Brown

I do not believe our farmers are prepared to submit to such legislation as that. In that connection may I read a short letter written by a farmer to the Winnipeg Free Press:
Eighty miles north of Carlyle there is an Indian reserve. An agent and a farm instructor tell the Indians what to do and how, when and why to do it.
They are told what to plant and how and where to plant it. If they have something to sell they must secure a permit from the agent. If they are short of funds the agent may give them an order for goods on the local store and later he will sell their produce to foot the bill.
How about the farmer under the new marketing Act? Well, he is placed squarely on the 'Indian list." If the government chooses to take the farmer-and' why should it be embodied in the act if they never intend to use it-every thing I have described as applying to the Indian, will apply to the farmer.
He will not be allowed to raise a chicken, cow or pig or sell a bushel of wheat or a dozen of eggs without a permit from some government agent.
Are the farmers of western Canada going to stand for that kind of treatment? If they do then we can come to but one conclusion, that the government is fully justified in putting them on the "Indian list."
G. W. Stockton. Carlyle, Sask., April 10, 1934.
I am prepared to go a certain distance to meet a situation such as has developed in British Columbia in connection with fruit. Recognizing as I do the rights of majority control, I am prepared to go some distance in that regard, although I do not like to interfere with personal liberty. In view of the situation which has developed in that province, if by a large majority the fruit growers are willing to do certain things and they obtain the sanction of the provincial government, as a member of this House of Commons I would be willing to go as far as our constitution will allow to give them the right to handle their produce in the manner they themselves have decided it should be handled. I am willing to go that far. Then, if a majority of the farmers on the prairies decide to adopt some kind of board to control their live stock or their dairy produce, while as a citizen of Manitoba I might and undoubtedly in some cases would object, as a member of this house I should feel obligated under the circumstances I have described to give them the right to do so. That is an entirely different thing, however, from beginning at the top and giving to this or to any government or any board the right to take all these matters under its control. I am entirely opposed to parliament resigning its powers into the hands of any board or executive.
Reference has been made to the British Marketing Act. I am not going to say I

am in favour of that act. England is a country entirely different from Canada, and the circumstances obtaining there are quite different from those obtaining in this country. That which may suit England, a small compact country, may not suit us at all. Therefore at the moment I am not prepared to say that I would support legislation in this House of Commons simply because it followed closely the British marketing legislation. 1 am prepared, however, to take specific cases as they arise and to deal with them as the circumstances demand. I am not prepared to throw over our established method of doing things and at once to institute a new method. I believe in orderly progress, here a little and there a little, dealing with situations as they arise. That to my mind is the attitude which will commend itself to the people of Canada.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the government on the attitude it has taken as reflected in the marketing bill now before the house. For two or three years we have been talking about arrangements which should be made for the orderly marketing of our produce. We are now trying to put through this house a bill which will bring about that which we desired. Several lawyers opposite have expressed their opinions, and we have had opinions from other hon. members opposite who know nothing about marketing or the conditions under which the eastern farmers operate. They are familiar with the selling and marketing of wheat, but they are totally ignorant of and do not understand the facts and conditions affecting the marketing of the produce of eastern farmers.
Some members of the opposition have spoken of this as a bill with teeth in it.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: False teeth.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
We require a bill with
teeth in it, double teeth all around in both jaws. At the present time the packers and the commission men have absolute control of the marketing of the farmers' products in the east, and anything that can be done to take control out of their hands I am willing and glad to support. The minister distinctly stated when introducing the bill that he did not regard it as perfect, but that it was a beginning. I should like to know what kind of bill could be brought in by the minister or by anybody on this side of the house that hon. gentlemen opposite would agree to. They have not agreed to a single clause of this marketing bill; they have found fault with it all.

Marketing Act-Mr. Picket
I just want to give a few facts that I know. This criticism from the other side of the house is simply for political purposes. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) stated a few moments ago that we have grading acts at the present time and he knew of no one who was opposed to them except perhaps the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) and eastern farmers. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am an eastern farmer and I am opposed most strongly, not to the grading acts themselves, but to their administration and operation. That is what I am opposed to.
Because of the grading acts and because of the arbitrary action of the packers and commission men in the cities the price of eggs, for example, fluctuates. When the farmer has none to sell the price is high, but during the producing season all summer the price is depressed. I contend that the price of a dozen eggs or a pound of butter in this country should never go below twenty-five cents. The price should be more or less uniform. Why should the price be depressed?
In the spring of the year when the farmer begins to produce butter, which is his chief commodity, the commission men and the packers arbitrarily depress the price and keep it depressed all summer just so long as the farmer is producing, and while the price is kept low they fill up their warehouses. But the minute the farmer stops producing, up goes the price, and butter will be selling at forty cents a pound and eggs at fifty cents a dozen when the farmer has none to sell. That is the condition of the eastern farmer, and I say that these marketing conditions should be regulated. The packers in the cities know perfectly well that on all the butter and eggs they buy during the summer they are going to double and treble their money. In this country we consume all the butter and eggs that we produce. We are not exporting butter and eggs, and why should the packers be allowed arbitrarily to depress prices to suit their own purposes, in order to make millions next winter? You will see that they will repeat the old trick pretty soon now; you will see butter and eggs soon go down to the lowest point. Eggs will be selling for ten or twelve cents a dozen this summer and the packers will be filling up their cold storage warehouses at that price. That is what the farmer is up against. And the packers will buy butter at fifteen and sixteen cents this summer and sell it at 30 to 35 cents a pound next winter. Is there any justice in that? Do we not need a marketing board? I should think we do, and one with teeth in it.
The condition of the eastern farmer is almost as bad in marketing beef and meat
products as it is with respect to butter and eggs. The man in the city does not realize it. He gets his meat at very reasonable prices, but the man in the country pays right up to the hilt.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: What about the man in the city?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: You can get it much cheaper than I can get it in my village where we are producing the goods; you can get it twenty-five to thirty per cent cheaper. It a man in the eastern townships has a beef animal to sell he cannot sell it to the local butcher because there is none; the local butcher has been put out of business by the packers. The small local butcher might operate for a little while until the packer comes along and puts somebody right down beside him and gives him his meat until the other man is put out of business. That is what they are doing. I tell you straight that I can go on St. Catherine street and buy meat products twenty-five to thirty per cent cheaper than I can in any small village in the east.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: That must be the cheaper meats.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Every kind of meat, fish and everything. In the larger towns like Granby, Waterloo and Farnham, where there is some competition provided by the Dominion stores and Atlantic and Pacific stores, prices are a little more reasonable, but in the smaller towns where there is no competition and the packer has control we pay right up to the hilt. The farmer cannot sell his beef animals to the butcher; he has to sell them to the local agent of the packer, who transports them to Montreal where they are slaughtered, and we have to pay the transportation charges in and out, and one or two abattoir charges are charged back to us.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Is this bill going to remedy that?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: The packer is the cause of it all.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Is this bill going to fix that up?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
It should. Let us try it. I am willing to try anything.
Last session I introduced a resolution into this house on behalf of the United Farmers of Danville in the province of Quebec in regard to the sale of reactors. I want to say a word or two on that subject. The request at that time was that all these reactors should be sent direct to the fertilizer factory. Let me give the house my experience. In 1928
Marketing Act-Mr. Picket

or the early part of 1929, on one of my farms I lost five head of cattle. They were large Holsteins. A neighbour also lost five cattle, but his were common grade cattle. They were were not nearly as large as mine and not in as good condition. His cattle and mine were sent to Montreal on the same day. This neighbour of mine telephoned to one of the inspectors of the department in Montreal and told him that he was shipping cattle. He asked him to go down to the abattoir to see that he got somewhere near their value. A man was sent down and this neighbour received $25 per head for his five head. My five head went through the local dealer; I had no one at the abattoir and I received only $24 for the five.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Exactly the same cattle?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mine were better. In July last year a neighbour of mine sold a three year old heifer for beef. He was sending milk to the city and he feeds all his cattle quite heavily. At the same time he was selling two or three hogs and some young cattle. When he got to Montreal the buyer came round to look at his animals and the price offered for the hogs and calves was quite acceptable. He then asked about his heifer and the dealer said he would pay $20 for the animal. Under the rules I could not repeat the language of the owner of the heifer when he heard the price offered. He said, "Are you trying to be a philanthropist, or what"? The dealer told him he considered the animal was worth more than $20 but that they had to sell the animal. That is the position they take. Last December I lost four head on another farm and all I could get was $4, just enough to buy a can of disinfectant. That is the position we in eastern Canada are up against. I do not know anything about the wheat situation and I am sorry that the wheat market is as it is. I do not know whether this proposed marketing board can help out in disposing of the wheat, but I do know that it can help in eastern Canada to dispose of everything that we produce.
The hon. member for Lisgar referred to the grading acts, and it is these very acts that these people take advantage of. I am not against grading; I believe our goods should be graded, but I do object to the manner in which these grading acts are used by the middleman in order to beat the farmer. I have mentioned already the case of eggs which I returned to Montreal. That could be repeated any day. You can send into the city and get a case of eggs and then

when you send it back you will not get more than half what you paid for them; the grading will be depressed by fifty per cent. Such a condition of things should be readjusted. The hon. member for Lisgar said that there was no emergency and that the powers granted under this act were too great to be given to any board. I contend that emergency exists and has existed for some time.
The principal products of the farmer in the east are milk, cream, butter, eggs and pork. I think we are in a fair way to getting some adjustment in the matter of milk and cream. I understand a milk commission has been appointed in Ontario. We have one in Quebec which has power to set prices. The Minister of Agriculture for Quebec is to be highly commended for this action. We believe that the farmer will now get a fifty-fifty division of the consumer's dollar. I do not know what is going to be done in Ontario. As far as butter and eggs are concerned, the farmer does not get a fair deal and these are two of his principal products.
While I am on my feet I might say that I have always advocated the manufacture of more cheese and less butter, and I should like to tell the house why I am of that opinion. The price of cheese is regulated on the British market, but the price of butter is fixed in Montreal. The eastern townships farmer who sends his milk to a creamery does not receive more than fifty per cent of its value. The creamery does its own testing and weighing and the farmer has not a chance. Here is an instance of the way we are treated. Three years ago I was sending cream from one of my farms to a certain creamery and it was testing 35 per cent. The creamery changed hands and within six months the test had dropped to 22 per cent. I said to the man on the farm, "Joe, they are stealing your cream." He said, "I know they are, but what can we do about it?" I told him that I would have a different truck come into my yard every day or every week if necessary. Without my knowledge he sent his cream to Eaton's in Montreal and the first test showed 42 per cent. During the past two years it has never been below 40 per cent. That is what the farmer in the east is up against.
There is a contention which I have made before to which many take objection, namely that we make the poorest butter that reaches the British market. We are in a fortunate position in that we do not export any more than we import; we are able to consume all the butter that we can manufacture. I contend that in the east we should manufacture cheese entirely and let the west supply us

Marketing Act-Mr. Bradette
with butter. They make a good article, and butter manufacture adapts itself to the west. Milk is rather bulky, and as their factories are sparsely situated they would be able to manufacture butter much easier than cheese. As I said before, the price of cheese is regulated on the British market and we always receive a premium for our product. In 1903 or 1904 we sent over
247.000.	000 pounds of cheese while last year we sent only about 70,000,000 pounds. If we are not careful we are going to lose our cheese market. In 1903 or 1904 New Zealand sent hardly any, while last year they sent
250.000.	000 pounds; they have taken our place as far as quantity is concerned, but we still maintain our position as far as quality goes -we still obtain a premium on our cheese. It is hard for one man to go about the country and talk the farmers into making cheese. I do all I can, but I think the government should initiate a campaign throughout eastern Canada advising the farmers to make cheese. Instead of that, however, all governments for the past twenty-five years have advised the farmers to make butter, and especially to go into winter dairying. I never knew a man in this country to make a cent in winter dairying; it takes all summer to pay their winter grain bills. You cannot make money in the winter in this country in making butter.
I hope this marketing bill will extend to the grain business. We pay $24 or $25 a ton for bran while you can hardly give away wheat in the west. Someone is getting a great rake-off. Practically 95 per cent of the mill feed coming to Montreal from Fort William and Port Arthur comes by water; the water rate is 22 cents per hundred pounds while the rail rate is 44i cents. Yet when a farmer comes to Montreal for a car of mill feed he pays the 44J cent rate for it. The millers are exacting $4 on every ton they supply to the farmers. That is not right; it is not just, and I hope this situation will be remedied under this bill. It would be a great help to us and would also help the western farmers to ge.t rid of some of their mill feed and wheat.
I do not think I have anything more to say, Mr. Speaker, with regard to this bill, though when it is considered in committee I will gladly take part in the discussion of the various sections. In introducing the bill the minister stated that perhaps it was not perfect, so some objection may be raised to some of the sections. I do not see, however, any reason for the wholesale onslaught that we have witnessed from the other side.
It is unreasonable, and I cannot understand it. It has not come from farmers; not a farmer across the way has had anything to say about it.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: What about the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) ?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: The hon. member for Lisgar is not a farmer; he is a wheat miner.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend what he thinks constitutes a farmer?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman may keep two or three cows, but probably they are dry most of the time.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I offer no excuse for taking part in this debate, Mr. Speaker; I do not feel that I need apologize to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. It seems to me that every time the opposition discusses questions of national importance we are accused of doing so for political reasons. The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel) made the same suggestion, but I feel quite at ease in discussing the bill which is before the house. I do not think hon. gentlemen opposite should cast such reflections on the opposition; they always do so for political effect.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Sure.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I challenge the hon. gentleman who just spoke to name one instance where that has been the case.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: I think all the opposition that has been expressed to this bill up to the present time has been for political effect.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
That is certainly a nice statement for a member of parliament to make on the floor of this house; that is a reflection on all the representatives here, because it applies to every hon. member.
As a retailer in the town of Cochrane for a quarter of a century I am going to deal with the statement made by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi to the effect that the packers are trying to put out of business the retailers and small butchers. I have handled meat, but I yet have to see a packer try to put out of business a single retailer in northern Ontario. I hold no brief for the packers; I have tried to pay my bills, though they charge as much as they can, but I must say that in my opinion the hon. member has no right to insinuate that in any section of the country the packers have tried to put the small butchers out of business.
Marketing Act-Mr. Bradette

Following the words of the minister in introducing the bill, every hon. member, whether on this or on the other side of the house, is perfectly in order in giving his views on this legislation, so that the bill may be in proper form when it is reported by the committee. At page 2205 of Hansard the minister said:
I had hoped that there would be little controversy in connection with this bill. No one realizes and appreciates more than I do the fact that it is far from perfect.
Surely that is an invitation to discuss the bill. There are two kinds of criticisms, destructive and constructive, and I challenge any hon. member opposite to say that the criticism that has come from this side of the house has been destructive. Surely the speeches of the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher), the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) and the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) could not be said to contain destructive criticism. I repeat that hon. members are absolutely within their rights in discussing the merits of any bill. I remember that in the fall of 1930 it was said that the Prime Minister had to attend the imperial conference and we were urged to put the legislation through as quickly as possible. The same situation has existed on other occasions; scourges have been held over our heads to prevent us from discussing matters of national importance. That is why I, as the humble representative of the riding of North Timiskaming I intend to present the viewpoint of the consumer, and I do not apologize for doing so. The minister said, at another place:
The first is that it must be sound, the second that it must be simple of operation, and the third that it must be practical.
Surely two hundred and forty-five men, elected by the electors of this country, have as much right to advise the Minister of Agriculture as the experts, whether in agriculture or in industry, who haye been advising him for at least two months, especially since this discussion was invited by the minister himself when he presented the bill. In the last paragraph of the minister's speech I find these words:
I do trust, however, that this bill will be discussed in the spirit in which it is presented. In its preparation we have endeavoured to obtain all the points of view possible so far as the organized producers were concerned, at the same time discussing it frankly and freely with those -whose business primarily has been that of marketing.
Surely, then, I have the right to present the point of view of the consumer. It is true that in my section of the country we have

primary producers, but they are mainly engaged in the mining industry and farming, so this bill does not apply to them. It is true that a certain number of our population have graduated from the ranks of settlers to become farmers, but they are not in a position as yet to export anything to other countries. But we are all consumers, and our point of view apparently has not been considered in connection with this bill. Apparently the consumers have not been asked what they think of the bill; apparently the consumers have not advised the government or the minister in connection with the act. Representing a section of the country where we are all practically consumers I know from my past sad experience that when any new restrictions or regulations are imposed by the government we in northern Ontario have to pay the piper as a result. I well remember some restrictions which were imposed by this government-

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman allow me a question? Is there anything political about his speech now?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Certainly not; I have
the right to represent my own riding.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
You are living among
consumers.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I have some knowledge of farming, but I am giving the viewpoint of the consumers. I maintain that in this bill there should be incorporated the viewpoint of the consumer. I well remember when I was sitting on the government side the ridicule that was often cast upon the so-called Consumers' League, because the consumers had the audacity to be represented before the tariff board. Surely on such an important matter as this new legislation which is so sweeping in its character and which goes to the very root of the national and personal life of practically every citizen in Canada, the consumer should have been asked for his advice.
Again I repeat that so far as the mining sections, the northern sections of the three western provinces and practically the whole of British Columbia are concerned, any new regulation that is imposed upon any of our activities, whether mining or farming or otherwise, means simply another load put upon the shoulders of the consumer. Some hon. members might be astonished if they knew the prices we have to pay in nothern Ontario since the seasonal tariffs were put on imported fruit and vegetables, and they would be more surprised at the price we have to pay for Canadian fruit. The price is simply ridicu-

Marketing Act-Mr. Bradette
lous and unless people are well to do they find it impossible during the winter months to buy lettuce, celery and other foods that are supposed to be good for the health of the people at such a season. It all amounts to this, that in a bill of this character apparently-and I say this in all sincerity-the viewpoint of the consumer has not been considered.
No doubt a certain amount of good could be said about this legislation, and I repeat that it shows a trend of thought which has been in progress for the last ten years not only in Canada but throughout the civilized world. We are speaking more and more of planned economy and in terms of government interference in all activities; in fact, if one studies the movements and revolutions that have occurred in Europe, their origin has always been with the idea in the minds of the mass of the people that the capitalistic or industrial system had been so faulty that the controlling authority which would be set up through those evolutions should take upon itself the responsibility of all social and national activities. The same thing applies to some extent to this bill, and again I want to make myself very clear in this, that I believe the intent of the bill is good. There is no doubt in my mind that the capitalistic system has failed and at the present time it is having to bear the results of its own sin. I have no doubt that the citizens of this country worthy of the name are willing to give a very thorough study to this bill and this is also true of every newspaper, every institution, every one of our provinces and every one of our premiers; they have already made comments on the bill. Therefore any hon. member, whether on the government side or in the opposition, is entitled to voice his opinion, always with the one idea in mind that out of this measure something tangible will emerge that will give the people greater prosperity and comfort than they have had.
Some comparisons have been made between this bill and the British Agricultural Marketing Act of 1931. There are some slight similarities, but as has been so well pointed out by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher) and the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley), those similarities are not so great as to justify the impression being created that the same marketing bill they have in England would be good in Canada. The reason for this is very simple. In Great Britain they have only one central government, one that is all-powerful so far as national legislation is concerned, while here we do not have the same situation.
Here we have provincial governments, and we cannot get over the fact that they are already in existence. There has already been discussion of the bill by some of the premiers, some being in favour of it and others against it. Therefore it is obvious that conditions surrounding the creation of the two bills are entirely different, and for the reasons I mentioned a few moments ago the British act would be impossible of application in this country.
We must not get away from the fact that the Hon. Mr. Elliot, Minister of Agriculture in Great Britain, is in a different position from our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) so far as the farmers are concerned. Mr. Elliot wants to make Great Britain self-sustaining as regards the products of the farm while in Canada we are faced with a different situation; here our farmers find themselves in the position where they have a surplus which must of necessity be exported, whereas in Great Britain they have no surplus, but a shortage. Thus, in discussing this bill we must see that we are on firm ground and not try to make comparisons too closely.
After reading the bill very carefully several times and after having studied throughly the NjRA. of the United States, I believe that there is between the two a number of similarities; in several clauses the wording is practically the same, but the difference is this: the N.R.A. goes into all the activities of the United States while our marketing legislation singles out only certain activities of our national life, chiefly agricultural; it leaves out entirely mining, the automotive industry, cottons and other textiles. In a word, it leaves out the industries as we understand and know them. I am not aware of the reason for that. Is it because the government have thought, perhaps wisely, perhaps unwisely- this is not for me to say now-that by the high tariffs they have given to those industries, those sheltered industries, for the last four years, they have done all they can for them while during all that time the farmers have been left to look after themselves, and that this legislation is to be a sop for the farmers. That question I will leave the house to answer. The similarity between the present bill and the N.R.A. holds good only so far as the farmers are concerned. If the government contend it is such a good measure as the minister says it is going to prove; if it is so good for the farmer, the fisherman and the lumberman, why is the miner left out and why should the same principles not be applied to all our national activities? That I do not know.



Marketing Act-Mr. Bradelle
In this discussion we should not get away from the fact that the present bill is no more and no less than planned economy. Everyone knows that the capitalistic system has sinned, but we should also remember that the capitalistic system has proven to the world that through its inventions, its ability of administration and management it could supply all the requirements of the civilized world. Surely to-day the same men who were responsible for that situation, who could develop the creative power of producing plenty should at this time without any drastic measure be able to do their part in the national scheme without compulsory power being given to certain men or boards, and they certainly should be Canadians enough to give a lead to this country during the present time of stress.
The hon. member who preceded me has cited several cases of butter, eggs, meat, cattle and so on, where he has told us there were inspections and over-inspections. So to-day we have machinery sufficient to a large extent for a planned economy, but the trouble is that no matter how many laws are put on the statute book, no matter how many regulations you may have, if the government has not the energy and sincerity to enforce them they remain a dead letter. That applies to this measure; unless the government is ready to see that it has full application.
In every section of this country there has been a deep interest in and serious discussion of this bill. This morning I received a letter which I believe was sent to every member of parliament by the chamber of commerce of Montreal, asking the government to make certain amendments to this bill. Again it comes to the point I mentioned a moment ago; surely if chambers of commerce, cooperative and other organizations, find it desirable to advise the government on such matters, it is the bounden duty of members of parliament in their humble way to present to the government their views on this very important measure. Therefore I want to speak brief!}' of certain features of this bill, features which in themselves may seem practicable and fairly innocent, but I believe this is the time and place to bring forward any amendments which to us seem desirable. In fact the minister in his admirable speech in introducing it left the door wide open for full discussion, he was quite open-minded, he said the bill was not absolutely perfect, that it might involve some anomalies. Take for example subsection 2 of section 3:
The board shall consist of such number of persons as the governor in council may from time to time determine, and such member shall
fMr. Bradette.]
hold office during pleasure and shall receive such remuneration as the governor in council shall determine.
The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) has dealt with that. It simply means that in a matter of such national importance the power of control is taken from the parliament and given to a board. That is not the British parliamentary system as we understand it. Some hon. members may say that in Italy they have something similar to that, but Italy is under a dictatorship while in Canada the government is still supposed to be controlled by the representatives of the people. The point so well presented by the hon. member for Lisgar is that it would simply mean that in practice all our social and industrial activities will be taken out of the control of parliament. The members of this assembly are elected to represent the people, their wishes and their sentiments, but by this bill the control of some of our most important national activities will be taken away from this forum. Take again subsection 5 of section 3:
The board may, with the approval of the governor in council, employ such technical, professional and other officers and employees as the board may deem necessary or desirable, and such persons shall receive such salaries or remuneration as may be fixed by the board with the approval of the governor in council.
That again is invading a field which should not be invaded. The agricultural marketing act of Great Britain is in a different situation in that respect. The hon. member who preceded me has shown that we have inspection and overinspection as far as primary production is concerned, there are too many inspectors at the present time trying to advise the producers. Yet over and above the existing machinery this bill proposes to erect another board with another set of officials; it is certainly bureaucracy with a vengeance. Our provinces have machinery for looking after these matters, there are marketing boards and cooperative societies in many sections of the prairies; we have the national research council which has cost millions of dollars and is doing good work. What would be the necessity for that organization under this board? It would seem that it would have to come under it or practically not function. I believe that section should be entirely struck out. Overlapping of that nature would cost the ratepayers of this country a lot of money. It would do nothing to lessen the price to the consumer or increase the profit of the producer. I have no grudge against government employees, but we must avoid bureaucracy, and any overlapping by

Oaths of Allegiance Act
now regulations will simply mean added cost to both consumers and producers.
Then subsection 9:
The governor in council may from time to time authorize payment to the board, out of the consolidated revenue fund, of such sums of money as may be necessary for the purposes of this act.
Anyone who has studied the British parliamentary system will realize that here again one of the most important prerogatives of parliament is taken from it by that provision. I see the right hon. Prime Minister smile.

speechtext: Is it not true that this board is going to take money out of the public funds without the sanction of parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: There is no legislation that does not involve a curtailment of the unrestrained and unlimited liberty of everyone. That is what parliament is for.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: But subject to the control of parliament.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: If this board is all powerful, is to function by itself without the sanction of parliament, it will be using the public funds which should be under the exclusive control of this parliament; there is no avoiding that fact.
